section_1.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Graph
section_1.content: Define a planar graph as one that can be drawn in a 2D plane without edges crossing. Introduce the basic components: Vertices (V), Edges (E), and Faces (F), where a 'face' is an enclosed region (including the infinite outer region).
section_1.example: Visualizing a house shape: 5 vertices (the house outline + roof peak), 6 edges, and 2 faces (the interior and the exterior).

section_2.title: The Master Equation: Euler's Characteristic
section_2.content: Introduce Euler's formula: V - E + F = 2. Explain how this fundamental invariant holds true for any connected planar graph regardless of how messy the layout looks, provided no edges cross.
section_2.example: Apply the formula to a simple triangle: V=3, E=3, F=2. Calculation: 3 - 3 + 2 = 2. It holds!

section_3.title: Concept of Duality
section_3.content: Introduce the Dual Graph (G*). To create a dual, place a point (vertex) inside each face of the original graph and connect two points if their corresponding faces share an edge.
section_3.example: Visualize a 'Grid City'. Each city block is a face. By placing a park in the center of each block and connecting parks across streets, you create the 'Dual Park Network'.

section_4.title: Interplay of Duality and Euler
section_4.content: Show how duality maps components: The number of faces in the original graph becomes the number of vertices in the dual (F=V*). The edges remain the same (E=E*).
section_4.example: An animation showing a 'Triangle Graph' transforming into its dual 'Y-shaped Graph', highlighting how the central vertex of the dual corresponds to the outer face of the original.

section_5.title: Application and Conclusion
section_5.content: Summarize the utility of duality in circuit design and map coloring proofs. Reiterate that these tools allow us to simplify complex networks by viewing them through their dual 'mirrors'.
section_5.example: Imagine a drone delivery robot navigating a complex web of roads; it uses the dual graph to find the shortest 'corridor' path between the centers of city blocks.

            "bl": Dot(color=WHITE),

        pos = {
            "p": "B3",
            "tl": "C2",
            "tr": "C4",
            "bl": "D2",
            "br": "D4"
        }
        for k, v in nodes.items():
            self.place_at_grid(v, pos[k])
        
        # Edges (6)
        edges = VGroup(
            Line(nodes["p"].get_center(), nodes["tl"].get_center(), color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes["p"].get_center(), nodes["tr"].get_center(), color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes["tl"].get_center(), nodes["tr"].get_center(), color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes["tl"].get_center(), nodes["bl"].get_center(), color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes["tr"].get_center(), nodes["br"].get_center(), color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes["bl"].get_center(), nodes["br"].get_center(), color=WHITE)
        )
        
        graph = VGroup(edges, *nodes.values())

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(graph))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

                  nodes["tl"].animate.set_color("#FF0000"),
                  nodes["tr"].animate.set_color("#FF0000"),
                  nodes["bl"].animate.set_color("#FF0000"),
                  nodes["br"].animate.set_color("#FF0000"))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF0000")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(edges.animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FF00")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        face_rect = Polygon(nodes["tl"].get_center(), nodes["tr"].get_center(), nodes["br"].get_center(), nodes["bl"].get_center(),

        self.play(FadeIn(face_rect))

        self.play(Write(text_prop))
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#FFFF00")
